title: A Balanced Tree From a Sorted List

concept.title: Take the middle element as the root
body: A sorted list can be turned into a **balanced** binary search tree: choose the **middle** element as the root, build the left subtree from the elements before it and the right subtree from the elements after it, each time with the same rule. The two halves differ in size by at most one, so the tree has a height of about log2(n) and every search is fast.

body.code:
def build(a, lo, hi):                     # the tree of a[lo..hi]
    if lo > hi:
        return None
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2                  # with two middle elements, the left one
    root = TreeNode(a[mid])
    root.left = build(a, lo, mid - 1)
    root.right = build(a, mid + 1, hi)
    return root

body: This is **divide and conquer**: split the problem in two halves of nearly equal size and solve each half recursively. The rule "the left one of two middle elements" makes the answer unique (it is the lower middle, `(lo + hi) // 2`). The depth of the recursion is only log2(n).

statement: Build a height-balanced binary search tree from `n` increasing integers: the root of every subtree is the middle element of its part of the list (if the part has an even number of elements, the left one of the two middle elements), the left subtree is built from the elements before it and the right subtree from the elements after it. Print the tree in level order in the same form as a tree in the input (`N` for a missing child, no `N` at the end).
inputFormat: The second line has `n` different integers in increasing order.
outputFormat: The tree in level order on one line.
constraints: -10^9 <= every value <= 10^9, and the values are different and in increasing order

examples.note: The root is 0; the left part -10 -3 has the root -10 with the right child -3; the right part 5 9 has the root 5 with the right child 9: 0 -10 5 N -3 N 9.

hints: The root is the middle element: index (lo + hi) / 2.
Build the left subtree from the part before the middle and the right subtree from the part after it.
An empty part gives an empty tree.

import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


# Builds a binary tree from a level-order list of words; "N" marks a missing child.
def build_tree(vals):
    if not vals or vals[0] == "N":
        return None
    root = TreeNode(int(vals[0]))
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    i = 1
    while head < len(queue) and i < len(vals):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if vals[i] != "N":
            node.left = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(vals) and vals[i] != "N":
            node.right = TreeNode(int(vals[i]))
            queue.append(node.right)
        i += 1
    return root


# Prints a tree in the same level-order form ("empty" for no tree).
def print_tree(root):
    if root is None:
        print("empty")
        return
    out = []
    queue = [root]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        node = queue[head]
        head += 1
        if node is None:
            out.append("N")
        else:
            out.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
    while out and out[-1] == "N":
        out.pop()
    print(" ".join(out))

explanation: The middle element becomes the root; the two parts around it are turned into the left and the right subtree by the same rule.
solution.complexity: Time O(n), space O(log n) for the recursion.
